content:
Jesus, the Christian apologist says, is "the only begotten Son of God", begotten of the Father before all ages. The phrase comes from the King James rendering of the Greek word monogenes in the Gospel of John.

This article aims to provide context to that word, insha'Allah, in five points: what it means, how the New Testament uses it of ordinary people, what it says of Isaac, how modern translations render it, and how John 1:18 reads in the oldest copies.

"He begetteth not, nor is He begotten; and there is none like unto Him" (112:3 to 4).[1]

Thayer's lexicon defines monogenes as "single of its kind, only", used "of only sons or daughters (viewed in relation to their parents)".[2] The second half of the word belongs with genos, "kind", and the word names a thing that is the only one of its kind.

The ESV renders John 3:16 accordingly: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son" (John 3:16, ESV). It renders John 1:14 "the only Son from the Father" (John 1:14).

Luke uses the same word three times of ordinary families. The dead man at Nain was "the only son of his mother" (Luke 7:12); Jairus "had an only daughter" (Luke 8:42); a father begs Jesus, "look at my son, for he is my only child" (Luke 9:38, all ESV).

No one reads those verses as a doctrine about how the widow's son was generated. The word says that each was the only child of the parent.

The decisive case is Isaac. "By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son" (Hebrews 11:17, ESV). The Greek is monogenes.

Isaac was not Abraham's only begotten son. Ishmael was born first: "Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael" (Genesis 16:15, ESV).

So the word cannot mean "the only one begotten". In Hebrews it marks Isaac as the unique son of the promise, echoing "your only son Isaac, whom you love" (Genesis 22:2).

Strength: firm. The New Testament itself uses the word of a son who had an elder brother.

The Revised Standard Version of 1952 dropped "only begotten" and rendered John 3:16 "his only Son". Dale Moody defended the change in the Journal of Biblical Literature the next year.[3]

The ESV, NIV and most modern translations follow it. The King James wording survives in the creeds and in apologetics, where it does work the Greek does not do.

Some theologians still defend "begotten" for doctrinal reasons. The argument then rests on the creed of Nicaea, which came three centuries after John, and no longer on the word.

John 1:18 shows the doctrine pressing on the text. The ESV reads "God the only Son, who is at the Father's side" (John 1:18, ESV), following Papyrus 66 and Papyrus 75, which read monogenes theos; other manuscripts read "the only Son".[4]

Either reading says that the one who made God known is unique. Neither says how he came to be, and neither crosses the line the Quran draws: "It is not befitting to (the majesty of) Allah that He should beget a son" (19:35).[5]

We set out the wider case in Jesus is not God.

The bottom line

The lexicon defines the word as "only". Luke uses it of three ordinary children, and Hebrews uses it of Isaac although Ishmael was born first. Modern translations dropped "begotten", and the variant in John 1:18 reflects the doctrine rather than producing it.

"Only begotten" is a translation, and the Greek does not support it. "He begetteth not, nor is He begotten" (112:3).

Notes

  1. Quran 112:3 to 4, A. Yusuf Ali translation.
  2. Joseph Henry Thayer, A Greek-English Lexicon of the New Testament, entry 3439, monogenes.
  3. Dale Moody, "God's Only Son: The Translation of John 3:16 in the Revised Standard Version", Journal of Biblical Literature 72 (1953): 213 to 219.
  4. The ESV footnote at John 1:18 records the variant "the only Son"; Papyrus 66 and Papyrus 75 read monogenes theos.
  5. Quran 19:35, A. Yusuf Ali translation.
